a: you who judge the earth
p: The book opens by addressing the world's rulers, but its real readers were Jews in a Greek city.
b: The Greek hoi krinontes tēn gēn, "those who judge the earth," means rulers: kings and judges. Chapter 6 takes up the same address ("kings" and "judges of the ends of the earth," 6:1). The speaker will turn out to be the wise king of Israel (7:1-14; 9:7-8), so the book is cast as one king advising others. The phrase echoes the Greek Psalm 2:10, paideuthēte, pantes hoi krinontes tēn gēn, which the site's Plain renders from the Hebrew as "Rulers of the earth, learn your lesson" (Psalm 2:10). The real first readers were almost certainly not foreign kings but Greek-speaking Jews, most likely in Alexandria, for whom the address made faithfulness to God look like the highest kind of statecraft.
orig: οἱ κρίνοντες τὴν γῆν (hoi krinontes tēn gēn)

a: Those who do not test him find him
p: Testing God means demanding proof on your own terms, as Israel did at Massah.
b: The Law warned, "Do not put the LORD your God to the test, the way you tested him at Massah" (Deuteronomy 6:16), and Jesus answers the tempter with that verse (Matthew 4:7). Wisdom pairs the warning with the prophets' promise that God is found by those who seek him (Jeremiah 29:13; Isaiah 55:6). The ungodly of chapter 2 do exactly the wrong thing: they decide to "test" the righteous man to see whether God will save him (2:17-19).

a: Wisdom
p: The Greek sophia is feminine. Where Wisdom acts or is described as a person, the Plain gives her a capital W.
b: Sophia is the book's key word. Here it is already almost a person: it "comes into" a soul and "lives" in a body, and 1:6 calls it "a spirit that loves people." The Plain writes "Wisdom" with a capital where she acts or is described as a person, as here and fully in 7:22-8:1 and chapter 10, and lowercase where the word means the quality or learning ("wisdom and discipline," 3:11). The background is Proverbs, where Wisdom calls out in the streets and was with God at creation (Proverbs 1:20-33; Proverbs 8:22-31).

a: a soul that schemes evil
p: Psychē is the person's inner self. In this book the word carries more Greek meaning than Hebrew nephesh does.
b: The Greek Bible uses psychē for Hebrew nephesh, which often means simply "life" or "a living being" (Genesis 2:7). In Wisdom the word leans toward the Greek sense: the inner self that thinks, chooses, can be led astray (4:11) and lives on in God's hand after death (3:1). Here soul and body are paired: wisdom will not live in a soul that plans evil or a body that sin owns. The Plain says "soul" every time the Greek has psychē. How far the book shares Greek ideas of the soul is the subject of the card on chapter 3 and the topic page.

a: deep in debt to sin
p: Katachreos means 'heavily in debt.' Sin is pictured as a creditor who owns the body.
b: The adjective katachreos is a money word: a person "deep in debt," whose property is pledged to someone else. A body "deep in debt to sin" belongs to sin, the way a mortgaged house belongs to the lender. The same picture of sin as debt runs through Jewish and Christian prayer: "forgive us our debts" (Matthew 6:12). Paul uses a related image of sin as a master who pays wages (Romans 6:23).

a: holy spirit
t: A holy spirit, or the Holy Spirit?
p: The Plain writes 'holy spirit' in lowercase: here it is wisdom's spirit, though Christians heard more.
b: The Greek has no article and no capitals: hagion pneuma paideias, "a holy spirit of discipline." In the flow of 1:4-7 it is wisdom itself, the spirit that teaches, which cannot live with deceit. The same phrase "holy spirit" stands in Psalm 51:11 and Isaiah 63:10, where God's own presence is meant. The Douay-Rheims, from the Latin, prints "the Holy Spirit of discipline" and goes on "will withdraw himself," reading it as the Holy Spirit. The Plain keeps lowercase and saves the capital for 1:7, where the Greek says "the Spirit of the Lord."

a: it is put to shame when wrongdoing comes in
t: Put to shame, or driven out?
p: The verb elenchō usually means 'convict' or 'shame.' Here the spirit seems to be shamed away by wrong.
b: Elenchthēsetai, "it will be convicted," is odd with a holy spirit as subject. The sense seems to be that it is put to shame and so withdraws, the way an honest guest leaves a house when crime moves in. The KJV and Douay give the sense "will not abide." The same verb runs through the chapter for God's spirit and justice "convicting" the wicked (1:3, 1:8, 1:9), so the line may be a deliberate turn: the spirit that convicts others is itself insulted when wrong arrives.

a: a spirit that loves people
p: Wisdom 'loves people' (philanthrōpos), the word behind English 'philanthropy.'
b: Philanthrōpos means "loving humankind," the word behind English "philanthropy." The book uses it again of wisdom's spirit (7:23) and says the righteous must be the same (12:19). The New Testament uses the noun once of God: "when the kindness of God our Savior and his love for humankind appeared" (Titus 3:4). The line balances love with judgment: wisdom loves people, but that does not mean it lets slander go.

a: his innermost parts
p: The Greek says God is witness to a person's 'kidneys,' the Bible's seat of hidden feelings.
b: Literally "his kidneys" (nephroi). In Hebrew thought the kidneys held the deepest feelings and motives, the way English uses "heart" or "gut." The pair "kidneys and heart" is a fixed phrase for the whole hidden self: "You test the kidneys and the heart" (Jeremiah 11:20), and Jesus says "I am the one who searches kidneys and hearts" (Revelation 2:23). The Plain says "innermost parts" so the sense is plain.

a: For the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world
t: The Spirit that fills the world
p: This verse, in Latin, is the opening chant of the Mass of Pentecost in the 1962 Roman Missal.
b: The Bible already says God fills heaven and earth (Jeremiah 23:24) and that no one can get away from his spirit (Psalm 139:7). The second line, "what holds all things together," uses the language of the Stoic philosophers, who taught that a divine pneuma runs through the universe and holds it together. Wisdom borrows the phrase for the God of Israel. Paul says the same of Christ: "all things hold together in him" (Colossians 1:17). In Latin, Spíritus Dómini replévit orbem terrárum, the verse is the Introit, the entrance chant, of Pentecost Sunday in the Roman Missal of 1962.
orig: πνεῦμα Κυρίου πεπλήρωκεν τὴν οἰκουμένην (pneuma Kyriou peplērōken tēn oikoumenēn)

a: Justice
p: Greek Dikē, Justice, was a goddess who tracked down the guilty. Wisdom uses the image for God's justice.
b: The Greek has the article, hē dikē, "the Justice," and makes it the subject of a verb of pursuit. Hesiod calls Justice "the daughter of Zeus," who sits beside her father and "tells him of men's wicked heart" (Works and Days 248-264, Evelyn-White's translation). The people of Malta talk this way when the snake bites Paul: "Justice won't let him go on living" (Acts 28:4), where the same Greek word stands. Wisdom keeps the image but empties it of any second god: in the next verse the report goes "to the Lord" (1:9). The Plain capitalizes Justice to show the personification.

a: the low hum of grumbling
p: Grumbling recalls Israel in the desert, whose complaints the LORD heard and punished.
b: "Grumbling" (gongysmos) is the word the Greek Bible uses for Israel's complaints in the wilderness. "it sounded evil in the LORD's ears. The LORD heard it, and his anger burned" (Numbers 11:1). Paul draws the same lesson: "And do not grumble, as some of them grumbled, and were destroyed by the Destroyer" (1 Corinthians 10:10). The "jealous ear" is God's: he is zealous for his people and hears even what is said under the breath.

a: a mouth that tells lies kills the soul
p: The liar destroys his own soul. Wisdom treats sin as self-chosen death, the theme of 1:12-16.
b: The verb anairei means "kills, does away with." The soul killed is the liar's own. This leads straight into the next section: death is something people bring on themselves "by the wrong way you live" (1:12). In Wisdom "death" often means more than the end of the body: it is the loss of life with God, which the ungodly choose.
orig: στόμα δὲ καταψευδόμενον ἀναιρεῖ ψυχήν (stoma de katapseudomenon anairei psychēn)

a: For God did not make death
p: Wisdom says death was not God's work. Genesis and Paul agree that death came through sin, but say it differently.
b: Genesis does not say God made death: it comes as the result of disobedience (Genesis 2:17; Genesis 3:19). Ezekiel says God takes no pleasure in anyone's death (Ezekiel 18:32), and Wisdom echoes that in its second line. Paul says "death through sin, and so death passed to all people" (Romans 5:12) and calls death "the last enemy" (1 Corinthians 15:26). So Wisdom matches the 66 books here. What kind of death is meant is debated: Wisdom also knows that the righteous die (3:2; 4:7), so "death" in 1:12-16 and 2:24 may mean chiefly spiritual death, being cut off from God, or may include the death of the body; the text allows both. The Catechism quotes 1:13 and 2:24 in its teaching on the fall (Catechism 413).

a: Hades has no royal throne on the earth
p: Hades is the Greek Bible's word for Sheol, the place of the dead.
b: Hadēs was the Greek name for the underworld. The Greek translators of the Hebrew Bible used it for Sheol, the place of the dead (Psalm 16:10; Isaiah 28:15). Wisdom says Hades has no basileion, no "palace" or "royal rule," on earth: God made the world for life, and death is an intruder. The ungodly think the opposite: for them Hades is the end, and no one comes back (2:1).
orig: οὔτε ᾅδου βασίλειον ἐπὶ γῆς (oute hadou basileion epi gēs)

a: For righteousness
p: Wisdom has two words: athanatos 'immortal' (not dying) and aphthartos 'incorruptible' (not decaying). The Plain keeps them apart.
b: This one-line verse uses athanatos, "immortal." Its noun athanasia, "immortality," comes in 3:4, 4:1, 8:13, 8:17 and 15:3. Wisdom also uses aphtharsia, "incorruption" (2:23; 6:18-19), and the Plain keeps the two words distinct. It is not the soul that the verse calls immortal but righteousness: life with God lasts because the righteous belong to the God who lives. Whether the book thinks the soul is immortal by nature, or by God's gift to the righteous, is the question of the card on chapter 3. Paul uses both words together: what dies "has to put on immortality" (1 Corinthians 15:53).
orig: δικαιοσύνη γὰρ ἀθάνατός ἐστιν (dikaiosynē gar athanatos estin)

a: They made a pact with it
p: The phrase recalls the rulers of Jerusalem in Isaiah who boasted of a covenant with death.
b: Isaiah mocked the leaders of his day: "We have cut a covenant with death; with Sheol we have signed a pact" (Isaiah 28:15). The Greek of Isaiah uses synthēkas, the same word Wisdom uses here for "pact." There the leaders thought the deal would protect them. Here the ungodly treat death as a friend and an ally, and become its party (2:24). "Its side" translates meris, "portion, share": see the note at 2:9.
orig: συνθήκην ἔθεντο πρὸς αὐτόν (synthēkēn ethento pros auton)

a: pined for it
p: The verb means 'melt.' They either longed for death as for a lover, or wasted away in its company.
b: Etakēsan is from tēkō, "melt, waste away." Greek love poetry uses it for lovers who "melt" with longing, which fits "they thought of it as a friend." The KJV took the other sense: "they consumed to nought." Both are possible, and both say that the friendship with death is a slow ruin.

a: their reckoning was crooked
p: The speakers are never named. Their words fit Jews who had given up the Law, talking like Greek pleasure-seekers.
b: Chapter 2 is a speech put in the mouths of "the ungodly." Some details sound like the Greek philosophy of chance and pleasure linked with Epicurus: we came to be by accident, the soul is a spark, death ends everything, so enjoy life. Other details show the speakers are Jews: the righteous man accuses them of "sins against the Law" and of "failing the discipline we were raised in" (2:12). So they read best as a type of the Jew who had dropped the Law to get ahead in a Greek city, drawn as a warning, rather than as a portrait of one school. Their words also sound like a one-sided reading of Ecclesiastes (see 2:2). The book answers them in 2:21-3:9 and lets them confess their mistake in 5:3-13.

a: We came to be by accident
p: The ungodly sound like a one-sided reading of Ecclesiastes: life is brief, death ends all, so enjoy yourself.
b: Ecclesiastes can be heard behind this speech. Ecclesiastes also says life is short and a shadow, that the dead are forgotten, and that "There is nothing good for a person but to eat and drink and let himself see good in his toil" (Ecclesiastes 2:24). But Ecclesiastes adds, "I saw that this too comes from God's hand," and ends with God's judgment (Ecclesiastes 12:13-14). The ungodly keep the first half and drop God. Whether Wisdom means to answer Ecclesiastes itself, or only people who quoted it, cannot be proved; the two books share themes, not quotations.

a: our mind is a spark
p: The Greek logos here is 'reason' or 'thought,' not 'word.' The ungodly make the mind a mere side effect of the heartbeat.
b: The usual rendering of logos on this site is "word," but here it means the power to think. The ungodly picture the mind as a spark struck by the beating heart: when the heart stops, the spark goes out and the body falls to ash (2:3). Some Greek thinkers did teach that the soul was fire or fine matter that scatters at death. Wisdom puts this view in the mouth of people whose "reckoning was crooked" (2:1), and replies that God made the human being "for incorruption" (2:23).
orig: ὁ λόγος σπινθὴρ ἐν κινήσει καρδίας ἡμῶν (ho logos spinthēr en kinēsei kardias hēmōn)

a: the breath
p: Pneuma here is the life-breath, so the Plain says 'breath.'
b: The Greek is to pneuma, the same word that means "spirit" in 1:5-7. Here the ungodly mean only the air that keeps a body alive, which "spreads out" like air when a person dies. The Plain says "breath" (as at 15:11 and 16:14). Ecclesiastes says "the spirit goes back to God, who gave it" (Ecclesiastes 12:7); the ungodly see only the air thinning out.

a: It has been sealed shut
p: Death is pictured as a sealed tomb or a sealed document: no one can open it again.
b: Katesphragisthē, "it was sealed," uses the image of a seal pressed on a door, a jar or a legal document so that no one could open it without breaking it. For the ungodly, death is a closed case. The Gospels tell of the stone of Jesus' tomb being sealed (Matthew 27:66), and of that seal failing to hold.

a: this is what we get, and this is our lot
t: Whose side? The theme of the 'portion'
p: Meris 'portion' and klēros 'lot' tie the book together: each person belongs to God's side or to death's.
b: The ungodly say pleasure is their meris, "portion," and their klēros, "lot." The words return on purpose. They "deserve to belong to its side" (meris, 1:16); "those who take his side" (meris, 2:24) experience death; and in the end they are amazed that the righteous man's "share" (klēros) is "among the holy ones" (5:5). In the Psalms the faithful say the opposite: "The LORD is the share I was given, and my cup" (Psalm 16:5), where the Greek also has meris.
orig: αὕτη ἡ μερὶς ἡμῶν καὶ ὁ κλῆρος οὗτος (hautē hē meris hēmōn kai ho klēros houtos)

a: the widow
p: The ungodly target exactly the people the Law protects: the poor, the widow, the old.
b: The Law commands, "Never treat a widow or a fatherless child harshly" (Exodus 22:22), and tells Israel to rise before the gray-haired and honor the old (Leviticus 19:32). The speech moves from pleasure (2:6-9) to cruelty (2:10-11) to murder (2:12-20). Wisdom shows that once there is no judgment after death, the weak have no defense.

a: Let our strength be our law of righteousness
p: The ungodly adopt the Greek argument that the strong should rule and justice is what the strong decide.
b: Greek writers debated this view. In Plato's Gorgias, Callicles argues that by nature the stronger should have more than the weaker, and that laws are made by the weak to hold the strong back. Wisdom has the ungodly say the same. The Bible's answer runs the other way: God "has pulled rulers down from thrones and raised the lowly high" (Luke 1:52), and the book ends this section with the thrones of the mighty overturned (5:23).

a: Let's set a trap for the righteous man, because he is a nuisance to us
t: A line from the Greek Isaiah
p: The plot's opening words come from the Greek of Isaiah 3:10, which differs from the Hebrew.
b: The Greek of Isaiah 3:10 reads, "Let us bind the righteous man, for he is troublesome to us" (Dēsōmen ton dikaion, hoti dyschrēstos hēmin estin). Wisdom repeats the clause almost word for word, with "let us lie in wait" for "let us bind." The Hebrew of that verse is different; the site's Plain from the Hebrew reads "Say of the righteous: 'Good!'" (Isaiah 3:10). So Wisdom was reading the Greek Bible, and it builds its whole story of the persecuted righteous man out of Isaiah's Greek.
orig: ἐνεδρεύσωμεν τὸν δίκαιον, ὅτι δύσχρηστος ἡμῖν ἐστιν (enedreusōmen ton dikaion, hoti dyschrēstos hēmin estin)

a: sins against the Law
p: The righteous man accuses the ungodly of breaking the Law: they are Jews who have left it.
b: Only a Jew could be charged with "sins against the Law" and with "failing the discipline we were raised in" (paideia, here the upbringing of a Jewish home in the Law). The Plain keeps the site's word "discipline" for paideia, as in 1:5 and 3:11; here its sense is the training a child received. So the ungodly are Jews who have turned from the covenant, and the righteous man is a faithful Jew whose life shames them. In Alexandria, where the book was most likely written, Jews lived among Greeks, and some gave up the Law to rise in Greek society. The quarrel in chapters 2-5 is first of all inside the Jewish community.

a: child of the Lord
p: Pais means both 'child' and 'servant.' It is the word of the Greek Isaiah for the Servant of the Lord.
b: Pais can mean "boy, child" or "servant." Because the righteous man also calls God his father (2:16) and is called "God's son" (huios, 2:18), "child" fits here. But pais is also the word in the Greek Isaiah for the Servant: "my servant" (ho pais mou, Isaiah 52:13), who is despised, killed and then exalted. The early church called Jesus God's pais: "his servant Jesus" (Acts 3:13). Wisdom's righteous man walks the Servant's road, and both senses are heard.

a: fake coins
p: Kibdēlos is a counterfeit coin, or base metal passed off as silver.
b: A kibdēlos coin was fake, made of base metal. The righteous man treats the ungodly as counterfeits: they look like Jews but are not true metal. It stings because their whole program is to get ahead in the world of money and power (5:8).

a: If the righteous man is God's son
p: Matthew's crowd at the cross says almost what the ungodly say here.
b: At the cross the chief priests, scribes and elders mock Jesus: "He has put his trust in God, so God should get him free now, if he takes delight in him. After all, he said, 'I am God's Son'" (Matthew 27:43). The first half follows Psalm 22:8 (Greek Psalm 21:9, which uses the same verb for "rescue," rhyesthai, as Wisdom does). The second half, the taunt about being God's son, is closest to this verse. Whether Matthew knew Wisdom or both draw on the Psalm and on common Jewish language for the righteous as God's children is debated; the likeness is real either way.

a: Let's sentence him to a shameful death
t: Is this a prophecy of Christ?
p: Augustine read 2:12-21 as Jesus' passion. Read historically, it is a type of the persecuted faithful Jew.
b: Augustine quotes 2:12-21 in full and says that in this book "the passion of Christ is most openly prophesied" (City of God 17.20). Christians who follow him see the claim to know God and to be his son, the test by torture, and the shameful death as fulfilled in Jesus. Read historically, the passage is a story-type, built from Isaiah's Servant (2:12-13; 5:1-2) and the Psalms, about any faithful Jew killed by apostates, whose vindication comes after death. The two readings need not cancel: a Christian can read it as a pattern that Jesus fills. The Plain keeps the text as the ungodly's speech about "the righteous man" and leaves the Christian reading to the notes.

a: a visitation will come for him
p: Episkopē, 'visitation,' is God coming to look after someone: to rescue or to judge.
b: Episkopē means a visit by someone with authority to inspect and act. In the Greek Bible it is God's "visiting" his people, in rescue or in punishment. The ungodly sneer that by the righteous man's own claims God ought to show up for him. Wisdom picks up their word: "when their visitation comes" the righteous will shine (3:7); the barren woman will have fruit "at the visitation of souls" (3:13); "his visitation is with his holy ones" (4:15). Jesus weeps over Jerusalem "For you did not recognize the season when you were visited" (Luke 19:44).
orig: ἔσται γὰρ αὐτοῦ ἐπισκοπὴ ἐκ λόγων αὐτοῦ (estai gar autou episkopē ek logōn autou)

a: They did not know his mysteries
p: Mystēria are hidden plans. Here they are God's secret purpose for the righteous after death.
b: In Greek religion, mystēria were secret rites into which people were initiated. Wisdom uses the word for God's hidden plan, which the ungodly could not see: that suffering is not the end and that the righteous are rewarded beyond death (3:1-9). The New Testament uses "mystery" for a secret of God now made known (Romans 16:25). In Wisdom the secret is opened in the next chapter.

a: for incorruption
p: Aphtharsia is 'not decaying.' God made humans to share his own lasting life.
b: Aphtharsia, "incorruption," means being free from decay. Wisdom's answer to the ungodly is drawn from Genesis 1: God made the human being "in his image" (Genesis 1:27), and Wisdom reads the image as a share in God's own eternity. Incorruption is the purpose of creation, not a natural possession: 6:18-19 says keeping wisdom's laws assures incorruption, and incorruption brings one near to God. Paul uses the same word for the resurrection: "It is sown in decay and raised in what cannot decay" (1 Corinthians 15:42).

a: through the devil's envy
p: Set beside Genesis 3, the devil is the serpent of Eden. 1 Clement joins the envy to Cain's murder of Abel.
b: Diabolos, "slanderer," is the Greek Bible's word for the Accuser. Set beside Genesis 3, where death follows the serpent's lie, the verse makes the serpent the devil, acting out of envy of the humans made in God's image (2:23); Revelation later calls him "the ancient serpent who is called the devil and Satan" (Revelation 12:9). 1 Clement uses the verse in another direction: it speaks of the "envy, by which death itself entered into the world" and goes straight on to Cain and Abel (1 Clement 3:4-4:7), whose story has the first killing (Genesis 4:8). Paul says death came through Adam's sin (Romans 5:12); John says of the devil, "From the start he was a killer of people" (John 8:44).
r: Genesis 3:1-19; Genesis 4:3-8; Revelation 12:9; John 8:44; Romans 5:12; Hebrews 2:14

a: But the souls of the righteous are in God's hand
p: The Catholic funeral rite and Orthodox Vespers for saints both read 3:1-9.
b: This is the best-known passage of the book. In the Catholic Order of Christian Funerals, Wisdom 3:1-9 (or the shorter 3:1-6, 9) is one of the Old Testament readings, and 4:7-15 is another. In the Orthodox churches 3:1-9 is one of the Old Testament readings at Vespers on saints' feasts, such as the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste (9 March) and the Great Martyr George (23 April), as the Orthodox Church in America's calendar of readings lists them.

a: in God's hand
p: To be in someone's hand is to be in his care and power, beyond the reach of enemies.
b: "All his holy ones are in your hand" (Deuteronomy 33:3). The psalmist prays, "Into your hand I place my spirit" (Psalm 31:5), and Jesus prays the same words from the cross (Luke 23:46). Jesus says of his sheep, "nobody will snatch them from my hand" (John 10:28). Wisdom applies the image to the dead: the persecutors killed the body, but the soul is where no torturer can reach it.

a: no torment will touch them at all
p: Basanos is the word for the torture of 2:19. What the ungodly did to the righteous man cannot reach his soul.
b: Basanos was the word for torture used to question a prisoner, and the ungodly used it in their plan: "Let's question him with insults and torture" (2:19). The answer here is direct: that torment ends at death, and none can touch the soul in God's hand. The Greek uses the strong double negative ou mē, "never at all." The same word is used of the rich man "in torment" in Hades (Luke 16:23).
orig: οὐ μὴ ἅψηται αὐτῶν βάσανος (ou mē hapsētai autōn basanos)

a: Their going out
p: Exodos, 'going out,' became a word for death. Luke uses it of Jesus' death.
b: The Greek is exodos, the title of the second book of Moses. Here it means "departure" from life. Luke uses it of Jesus at the Transfiguration, where Moses and Elijah speak "about his exodus, the one he was going to complete in Jerusalem" (Luke 9:31), and Peter speaks of "my departure" (2 Peter 1:15). To fools death looks like a disaster; to God it is a journey out.

a: their hope is full of immortality
p: Wisdom speaks of immortality, not of bodies rising. Whether it also expects resurrection is left open.
b: Unlike Daniel 12:2 and 2 Maccabees 7, Wisdom never clearly speaks of dead bodies being raised. It speaks of souls in God's hand (3:1), of immortality (3:4) and of the righteous who "live forever" (5:15). Yet it also has a future moment, "When their visitation comes" (3:7), when the righteous shine, judge nations and confront their killers (5:1). This can be read as the soul's life with God, in a Greek frame, or the visitation and the standing up of 5:1 can be read as pointing to a resurrection the book does not spell out. The card on this chapter sets out how churches answer the question this raises.

a: like gold in a smelter's fire
p: Testing by fire burns away what is worthless and leaves the pure metal.
b: "Silver goes in the melting pot and gold in the furnace, but it is the LORD who puts hearts to the test" (Proverbs 17:3). Zechariah says God will "test them the way gold is tested" (Zechariah 13:9), and Peter tells suffering Christians their faith is worth more than gold "which perishes even though fire tests it" (1 Peter 1:7). Wisdom reads the death of the righteous the same way: not a punishment, but the proof of their worth.

a: like a sacrifice burned whole
p: The death of the righteous is pictured as the offering that was burned entirely for God.
b: Holokarpōma is the "whole burnt offering," the sacrifice of which nothing was kept back (Leviticus 1). God "took them to himself" the way he accepted such an offering. The image turns martyrdom into worship. 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees speak of martyrs' deaths in the language of sacrifice, and Paul uses it for the Christian life (Romans 12:1) and for his own coming death (Philippians 2:17).

a: dart through the straw like sparks
p: The righteous are fire and the ungodly are straw, an image from the prophets of judgment.
b: The prophets pictured God's people as fire and their enemies as stubble: "The house of Jacob will be a fire, the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau stubble" (Obadiah 1:18; compare Zechariah 12:6 and Malachi 4:1). The shining of the righteous recalls Daniel 12:3 and Jesus' saying, "Then the righteous will blaze out like the sun in their Father's kingdom" (Matthew 13:43). Here both ideas meet: the righteous shine, and they run like fire through the straw of the wicked.

a: They will judge nations and rule peoples
p: The book promises the martyrs a share in God's rule, as Daniel, Jesus and Paul do.
b: Daniel sees that "The judgment went to the holy ones of the Most High" (Daniel 7:22). Jesus promises the Twelve they will "sit on twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel" (Matthew 19:28), and Paul asks, "Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world?" (1 Corinthians 6:2). Revelation sees the martyrs reign with Christ (Revelation 20:4). Wisdom adds at once that "the Lord will be their king forever": the righteous rule under God, not in his place.

a: wait by his side in love
p: The Greek can mean 'the faithful in love will stay with him' or 'the faithful will stay with him in love.'
b: The words hoi pistoi en agapē prosmenousin autō can be grouped two ways: "the faithful will remain with him in love," or "those faithful in love will remain with him." Either way the righteous dead are not lost in a shadowy Hades but are near God. On "grace" see the gloss. The KJV adds a further line here; see the variant.
orig: οἱ πιστοὶ ἐν ἀγάπῃ προσμενοῦσιν αὐτῷ (hoi pistoi en agapē prosmenousin autō)

a: They paid no heed to the righteous
t: The righteous, or what is right?
p: Tou dikaiou can mean 'the righteous man' or 'what is right.' Both fit.
b: The Greek tou dikaiou is masculine or neuter: "the righteous one" (the man of chapter 2, whom they ignored and then killed) or "what is right." The Plain says "the righteous," which in English can carry either sense. Their punishment fits their reasoning: they reasoned that death ends all (2:1-5), and for them it brings nothing good (3:18).
orig: οἱ ἀμελήσαντες τοῦ δικαίου (hoi amelēsantes tou dikaiou)

a: Their wives are fools, their children are wicked
p: These lines seem to punish families for the sins of the ungodly. The book's real point is about their 'offspring' and future.
b: Read alone, 3:11-12 sounds as if wives and children share the guilt. But the section that follows (3:13-4:6) shows the point: the ungodly put their hope in many children, as the old blessing promised, and Wisdom says that line of hope is empty without virtue. The Bible elsewhere insists each person answers for his own sin (Ezekiel 18:20). Wisdom speaks in the broad strokes of proverb, where the wicked man's house falls with him (Proverbs 14:11).

a: For the barren woman who stays undefiled is blessed
p: In the Hebrew Bible childlessness was a grief. Wisdom, like Isaiah 54, calls the faithful barren woman blessed.
b: Children were the great blessing of the covenant (Genesis 1:28; Psalm 127:3-5), and barrenness a sorrow that God often reversed (Sarah, Hannah). Wisdom goes further than those stories: the barren woman who keeps herself pure is blessed as she is, and her "fruit" comes at the judgment. Isaiah prepared the way: "Sing for joy, you barren one who has borne no child!" (Isaiah 54:1). This goes beyond most of the Hebrew Bible but matches Isaiah and the New Testament, where Jesus and Paul honor the unmarried (Matthew 19:12; 1 Corinthians 7:32-35).

a: at the visitation of souls
p: The 'visitation' here is God's judgment of souls, when faithfulness bears its fruit.
b: See the note at 2:20 on "visitation." Here it is the time when God examines souls and gives each its reward. The Latin Vulgate reads "of holy souls" (animarum sanctarum), narrowing it to the righteous; the Greek has only "of souls." Her "fruit" is not children but the reward of a faithful life, the "fruit of good labors" (3:15).

a: So is the eunuch
p: The Law shut eunuchs out of the assembly. Isaiah and Wisdom promise them a place in God's house.
b: Deuteronomy 23:1 barred a castrated man from "the assembly of the LORD." Isaiah promised the opposite to the faithful eunuch: "in my house and inside my walls I will set up for them a marker and a name that is better than sons and daughters" (Isaiah 56:5). Wisdom follows Isaiah: the faithful eunuch gets "a share in the temple of the Lord," sweeter to him than children. In the courts of the ancient kings, eunuchs often served as officials. Jesus speaks of those who are eunuchs "because of the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 19:12), and the first Gentile convert in Acts is an Ethiopian eunuch (Acts 8:27-39). Wisdom here goes beyond the Law, as Isaiah does.

a: all the more to his heart's delight
p: Thymērestatos is a comparative: 'more pleasing to the heart.' The comparison is with sons and daughters, as in Isaiah 56:5.
b: The Greek thymērestatos is a comparative without a stated second term. The natural second term is "than children," since Isaiah's promise was a name "better than sons and daughters" (Isaiah 56:5). The KJV reads "more acceptable to his mind," the Douay "a most acceptable lot."
orig: κλῆρος ἐν ναῷ Κυρίου θυμηρέστερος (klēros en naō Kyriou thymēresteros)

a: will never reach full growth
p: Atelesta means 'unfinished.' It may mean they die young, or that they never become full members of the community.
b: Atelesta means "not brought to completion." In plant language (4:5) it is fruit that never ripens: these children do not reach maturity. The word was also used in Greek religion of people "not initiated" into the rites, so it may also mean that they never enter fully into the life of God's people. The point is the contrast with the righteous, who are "made complete" even when young (4:13).

a: on the day of the verdict
p: Diagnōsis is a legal word for a judge's hearing and decision.
b: Diagnōsis is a court word: the hearing of a case and the judge's ruling. Paul appeals to Caesar "for the verdict of the emperor" (Acts 25:21), where the same word stands. Here the judge is God, and the day is the final reckoning that 4:20-5:23 describes.

a: It is better to have no children and have virtue
p: Wisdom says a childless life with virtue outlasts a large family without it, because virtue is remembered.
b: Kreissōn ateknia met' aretēs, "better is childlessness with virtue." The Greek word aretē, "virtue" or "excellence," was the great word of Greek ethics and appears only rarely in the Greek Bible. Wisdom uses it to answer the old hope of living on through one's children: the righteous live on in memory with God and with people, and that memory is "immortality." The Latin Vulgate, which the Douay follows, reads this verse quite differently, in praise of a chaste generation; see the variant.
orig: κρείσσων ἀτεκνία μετὰ ἀρετῆς (kreissōn ateknia meta aretēs)

a: leads the victory parade
p: The picture is of the Greek games: the winner, crowned, leads a parade through his city.
b: The verbs are from the Greek athletic games: stephanēphorousa, "wearing the crown," and pompeuei, "marches in procession." A winner at the games came home crowned with leaves and led a parade. Here virtue is the athlete, and the prizes are "pure" (amiantos, "undefiled," the word used of the barren woman in 3:13). Paul uses the same picture: "They do it to receive a crown that fades. We do it for one that never fades" (1 Corinthians 9:25; compare 2 Timothy 4:7-8; Hebrews 12:1).

a: Grown from illegitimate cuttings
p: The ungodly's many children are pictured as weak grafts that cannot root.
b: Moscheumata are cuttings or slips from a plant, and notha, "bastard," describes children born outside marriage. The whole passage (4:3-5) is a picture of a plant that sprouts fast, has no roots, and is torn up by the wind. It is the reverse of the righteous man of Psalm 1, "like a tree set out by channels of water" (Psalm 1:3). Jesus says, "Any plant that was not planted by my heavenly Father will be uprooted" (Matthew 15:13).

a: But a righteous man who dies before his time
p: The older wisdom said long life was the reward of the righteous. Wisdom says an early death can be God's mercy.
b: Proverbs says "The fear of the LORD adds days, but the wicked find their years shortened" (Proverbs 10:27), and the Psalms say men of blood "will not reach half their days" (Psalm 55:23). So an early death could look like God's judgment. Wisdom answers the case that the older teaching left hard: a righteous person who dies young is "in rest." Isaiah 57:1-2 had already said the righteous is taken away "from the presence of evil" and "goes into peace." Wisdom builds on that text and goes beyond Proverbs, without contradicting it. This passage (4:7-15) is read in the Catholic funeral rite.

a: Understanding is a person's gray hair
p: Gray hair was the honor of the old. Wisdom says wisdom is the true gray hair.
b: "Gray hair is a crown of beauty, found by those who walk in righteousness" (Proverbs 16:31), and "old men's beauty is their gray hair" (Proverbs 20:29). Wisdom keeps the honor but moves it: the mark of age is understanding and a spotless life, which a young person can have.

a: He pleased God, and God loved him
p: The words match the Greek of Genesis 5:24 on Enoch, which is the reason to read this of him. Wisdom never names him.
b: The Greek Genesis says, "Enoch pleased God, and he was not found, because God moved him" (euērestēsen ... metethēken, Genesis 5:24). Wisdom uses the same two verbs: "pleasing" (euarestos) and "he was carried off" (metetethē). Sirach also says "Enoch pleased the Lord and was carried off" (Sirach 44:16), and Hebrews: "By faith Enoch was carried off, so that he did not see death" (Hebrews 11:5). Wisdom does not name the people it tells about (compare chapter 10), and the Greek has no "one": the subject is simply "he," the righteous man of 4:7. The verbal match is the reason to read the passage of Enoch, whose life was short by the long ages of Genesis 5. Rashi, the medieval Jewish commentator, reads Genesis 5:24 in a similar way: Enoch was righteous but easily swayed, so God took him early. Genesis Rabbah 25:1, which Rashi follows, also records a rabbi who judged Enoch more harshly.
orig: εὐάρεστος τῷ θεῷ ... μετετέθη (euarestos tō theō ... metetethē)

a: He was snatched away
p: Harpazō, 'snatch,' is the word Paul uses for believers caught up to meet the Lord.
b: Hērpagē is strong: "he was seized, snatched." God snatches the righteous away before evil can corrupt him. Paul uses the same verb: "we who are alive and remain will be caught up along with them in clouds, to meet the Lord in the air" (1 Thessalonians 4:17), and of being "caught up" to paradise (2 Corinthians 12:2-4). Wisdom is not describing a rapture; it means an early death, seen from God's side.

a: the spell cast by worthless things
p: Baskania is the 'evil eye,' a spell or bewitching. Paul uses the verb for the Galatians.
b: Baskania meant bewitchment, the power of the "evil eye" to harm what it looks on. Wisdom does not mean magic: the "spell" is the pull of worthless things that makes good things look dim. Paul writes, "You senseless Galatians! Who has put a spell on you?" (Galatians 3:1), with the verb from the same root. The margin of Codex Vaticanus explains the next verb, metalleuei, "undermines," with words meaning "digs up, digs out."

a: and so it hurried out from the midst of evil
p: The Greek verb has no stated subject. It is either his soul that hurried away, or the Lord who hurried him.
b: Espeusen, "hastened," has no stated subject. The nearest subject is "his soul": it hurried out of the wicked world, as if eager to go to God. But the subject may be "the Lord," who hurried him away (the KJV: "hasted he to take him away"). The Plain follows the nearer subject; either way the early death was not an accident but a rescue.
orig: διὰ τοῦτο ἔσπευσεν ἐκ μέσου πονηρίας (dia touto espeusen ek mesou ponērias)

a: but the Lord will laugh at them
p: The verb is the one the Greek Psalm 2 uses for God laughing at the kings who rebel.
b: "Seated in the heavens, he laughs. The Lord makes fun of them" (Psalm 2:4). The Greek of the psalm has ekgelasetai, the same verb as here. The ungodly laughed at the righteous man (5:3); now the laughter is turned on them. Wisdom began by addressing the rulers of Psalm 2 (see 1:1), and it echoes that psalm again here.

a: After this they will become corpses no one honors
p: Swete's Greek starts verse 19 here. The KJV puts this line at the end of verse 18.
b: Verse numbers came long after the book was written. Swete's Greek text, which the Plain follows, and the Latin Vulgate begin 4:19 with "After this they will become..."; the KJV ends 4:18 with these words and begins 4:19 at "For he will smash them." The words are the same either way. Ptōma can mean a "fall" or a "corpse": the ungodly who thought the dead were forgotten (2:4) become corpses no one honors.

a: When their sins are counted up
p: Chapter 4 ends in a courtroom: the sins are added up, and the ungodly's own deeds take the stand.
b: Syllogismos is a reckoning or adding up, like an account book. The lawless deeds "stand up to their face" and "convict" (elenchō) them, as witnesses do in court. The scene of chapter 5 follows: the righteous man stands, and the ungodly speak their confession. Compare the books opened before the throne (Daniel 7:10; Revelation 20:12).
orig: ἐν συλλογισμῷ ἁμαρτημάτων αὐτῶν (en syllogismō hamartēmatōn autōn)

a: Then the righteous man will take his stand
p: The scene of 5:1-8 follows the shape of Isaiah 52:13-53:12: the despised one exalted, and his enemies stunned.
b: Isaiah's Servant is despised and killed, then "he will be high and lifted up, and very exalted" (Isaiah 52:13), while kings fall silent at what they see (Isaiah 52:15). Wisdom tells the same story about "the righteous man": killed in chapter 2, he now stands boldly before his killers, and "they will be astonished" (5:2). The Greek verb, ekstēsontai, is the one the Greek Isaiah uses in 52:14 for the many who were appalled at the Servant. Read with the New Testament, 5:1-5 recalls Christ coming as judge, seen by those who pierced him (Revelation 1:7). On "the righteous man," see 2:12 and 2:20.
orig: στήσεται ἐν παρρησίᾳ πολλῇ ὁ δίκαιος (stēsetai en parrhēsia pollē ho dikaios)

a: Repenting
p: The ungodly finally see the truth, but their repentance comes after death, when it can only confess.
b: Metanoountes is the usual word for repentance, a change of mind. Here it is regret, not rescue: the ungodly admit they were wrong (5:6-7), but their life is over (5:13-14). Jesus' parable of the rich man and Lazarus also has a late discovery and a gulf that cannot be crossed (Luke 16:26), and the foolish young women find the door shut (Matthew 25:11-12). The Latin Vulgate adds a line after 5:13 that puts this whole speech "in hell"; see the variant at 5:14.

a: among the sons of God
t: Sons of God and holy ones
p: 'Sons of God' and 'holy ones' may mean the angels, or God's righteous people. The righteous man joins them.
b: In the Hebrew Bible "the sons of God" are often angels, the heavenly court (Job 1:6), and "holy ones" can be angels too (Daniel 7:18, where the meaning is debated). On that reading, the righteous man is counted among the angels, as Daniel says the wise will shine like stars (Daniel 12:3). But Wisdom also calls Israel God's "son" (18:13) and the righteous man claimed to be "God's son" (2:18), so the phrase may mean the faithful people of God. Either way the ungodly's mockery has turned: the man they tested as a pretended son of God is one.
orig: ἐν υἱοῖς θεοῦ ... ἐν ἁγίοις ὁ κλῆρος αὐτοῦ (en huiois theou ... en hagiois ho klēros autou)

a: No light of righteousness shone for us
p: Truth is a road, and righteousness is light and sun. The ungodly confess they walked in the dark.
b: The images are from the Psalms and prophets: God's word is a lamp on the path (Psalm 119:105), and "a sun of righteousness will rise, with healing in its wings" for those who fear him (Malachi 4:2). The KJV reads "the sun of righteousness" here as well; see the variant. John uses the same picture: "The light is shining in the dark, and the dark did not get hold of it" (John 1:5).

a: like a ship going across the heaving water
p: Three pictures, a ship, a bird and an arrow, show that the ungodly's life left no mark.
b: Proverbs wonders at "the way of the eagle in the sky" and "the way of a ship in the heart of the sea" (Proverbs 30:19), paths that leave no track. Job says his days "glide away with the papyrus boats" (Job 9:26). Wisdom turns these into the confession of the ungodly: the ship, the bird (5:11) and the arrow (5:12) all pass and leave nothing behind, and so did they.

a: like chaff the wind carries off
p: The picture is from Psalm 1: the wicked are like chaff the wind blows away.
b: The Greek chnous, fine chaff or down, is the word of the Greek Psalm 1:4, which the site's Plain from the Hebrew renders "they are like the husks the wind drives off" (Psalm 1:4). Wisdom adds frost, smoke and a guest who stays one day. Here the narrator speaks again, after the ungodly's speech ends in 5:13.
orig: ὡς φερόμενος χνοῦς ὑπὸ ἀνέμου (hōs pheromenos chnous hypo anemou)

a: But the righteous live forever
p: Wisdom's hope is eternal life with the Lord, as in the New Testament, though it does not speak of the body rising.
b: "Whoever does what God wills remains for all time" (1 John 2:17), and Jesus says, "Those who believe in me, even if they die, will live" (John 11:25). Wisdom agrees that the righteous dead live with God and that their reward is "in the Lord's keeping." It does not say, as Daniel 12:2 and the New Testament do, that their bodies will rise; see the note at 3:4. The Most High (Hypsistos) is a common title of God in Greek-speaking Judaism.

a: the beautiful crown
t: The crown from the Lord's hand
p: The righteous receive a kingdom and a crown, the reward the New Testament promises the faithful.
b: Basileion can mean "kingdom" or "royal crown"; it pairs with "diadem," the band a king wore. The New Testament promises "the crown of life" (James 1:12; Revelation 2:10), "the crown of righteousness" (2 Timothy 4:8) and "the wreath of glory that never withers" (1 Peter 5:4). Compare also the victor's crown of virtue in 4:2.
orig: τὸ διάδημα τοῦ κάλλους (to diadēma tou kallous)

a: the full armor
p: Wisdom's armed God follows Isaiah 59:17, and Paul's 'armor of God' follows both.
b: Isaiah pictures the LORD arming himself to save: "Righteousness he wore as his armor, with salvation as a helmet on his head" (Isaiah 59:17). Wisdom expands the list: zeal as the full armor (panoplia), righteousness as breastplate (5:18), judgment as helmet, holiness as shield (5:19), anger as sword (5:20). Paul gives the same armor to believers: "pick up all of God's armor" (Ephesians 6:13), with "righteousness put on as your breastplate" and "the shield of faith" (Ephesians 6:14-16). Panoplia is the word in both Wisdom and Ephesians. Whether Paul knew Wisdom or drew on Isaiah alone is debated; his list is closer to Isaiah's in some points (the helmet of salvation) and to Wisdom's in others (the shield).
orig: λήμψεται πανοπλίαν τὸν ζῆλον αὐτοῦ (lēmpsetai panoplian ton zēlon autou)

a: turn the created world into a weapon
p: God makes the created world his weapon. The theme returns in the Exodus chapters at the end of the book.
b: God uses creation as his army: lightning, hail, sea and rivers (5:21-22). The Bible knows this picture: "The stars fought from heaven" for Israel (Judges 5:20), and hail fell on the Amorites (Joshua 10:11). Wisdom will develop it at length when it retells the plagues: creation serves its Maker by punishing the wicked and sparing the righteous (16:24; compare 16:17 and 19:6). This matches the Bible's picture of the Divine Warrior.

a: Bolts of lightning will fly straight to the mark
p: God's lightning is pictured as arrows shot from the bow of the clouds.
b: The Psalms and prophets give God a bow and arrows: "He let his arrows fly and scattered them; he shot lightning in plenty and threw them into panic" (Psalm 18:14; compare Psalm 7:12-13 and Habakkuk 3:11). The hail as from a siege machine (5:22) recalls the hail of the Exodus plagues (Exodus 9:23-25).

a: A wind of power
p: Pneuma dynameōs could be 'a mighty wind' or 'the Spirit of power.' The Plain keeps it as wind with power.
b: The Greek is pneuma dynameōs. Since it "blows them away like a whirlwind," it reads most naturally as a mighty wind, the last of the forces of nature God sends. But pneuma is also the spirit that fills the world (1:7), and the breath of God in the Bible can blow down the wicked: "the breath of his lips will put the wicked to death" (Isaiah 11:4). Wisdom uses the same phrase in 11:20, where the wicked could have been "winnowed" by the pneuma of God's power, with the same verb as here (likmaō). The Plain says "a wind of power" so that both senses can be heard.

a: tip over the thrones of the mighty
p: The section ends with rulers falling, which leads into the warning to kings in chapter 6.
b: The ungodly said, "Let our strength be our law of righteousness" (2:11). The section ends with that strength undone: the thrones of the powerful are overturned. Mary sings, "He has pulled rulers down from thrones and raised the lowly high" (Luke 1:52). Chapter 6 then turns to the kings and rulers of the earth with a warning, picking up the address of 1:1.
